title: Decoration of N-functionalized graphene nanoflakes with copper-based nanoparticles for high selectivity CO<sub>2</sub> electroreduction towards formate
abstract: The present electrocatalyst consists of copper and copper sulfide nanoparticles dispersed on graphene nanoflakes (GNFs), a stack of 5 to 20 highly crystalline graphene layers having typical side lengths of 100 by 100 nm. Plasma-based functionalization is used for adding covalently bonded nitrogen sites on the surface of the GNFs to a level of up to 2 at%. The catalyst nanoparticles are synthesized through wet chemistry, where graphene and a copper sulfate salt are mixed in a solvent and dried prior to pyrolysis under inert atmosphere at 700 °C. The amount of copper added to the carbon support is well controlled through this method, and is comprised between 20 and 50 wt%. Tests made towards the electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide show these catalysts generate a faradaic efficiency of up to 42.5% toward liquid products at -0.6 V vs RHE, with a high selectivity for formate. The performance of the catalysts is mostly driven by the amount of the copper sulfide phase rather than the metallic copper content, and competes with similar catalysts found in the literature for a fraction of the metal content.

1. Introduction
Strategies are put forward to reduce the emission of greenhouse gas (GHG), particularly carbon dioxide. These include, but are not limited to: the energy transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources;[1] energy storage systems;[2] promoting collective transportation and electric vehicles;[3] protecting and multiplying the number of green spaces as natural carbon storage systems;[4] making systems and processes more energy efficient.[5]
Time for implementation, cost, and political willingness are all constraints for a worldwide implementation of these strategies. It is unlikely the Paris agreement requirements will be met if no additional measures are taken, including active carbon and capture storage (CCS) and possibly geo-engineering. This agreement indicates that the global temperature rise should not exceed 1.5°C above the pre-industrial era temperature.[6]
Large scale CCS projects are being developed presently in order to curb the greenhouse gas emission. It is projected that the 21 main projects worldwide will have a capture capacity of 37 million tonnes per annum in 2018, the equivalent of the emission of 8 million cars.[7] A total of around 2,500 of such facilities would need to operate in 2040 to meet the Paris agreement requirements.[7] However, the main application of the CCS facilities is Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR). EOR is a technique where supercritical carbon dioxide, in the present case, is injected in an oilfield to improve the oil extraction.[8] The net carbon benefit of CCS is thus decreased, and it is estimated that only 10 to 25% of the CO2 is permanently sequestered through EOR.[9]
Extensive research has been made in the last decades on the CO2 conversion toward valuable products. CO2 is a highly stable and weakly reactive molecule. The process for its conversion is thus energy intensive. Different methods to convert CO2 exist, such as plasma[10] or photocatalytic[11] based techniques, but the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 is the most promising technology.[12] A catalyst is required to lower the energy requirements for converting CO2. Some transition metals used in the CO2 electroreduction have a
tendency to produce carbon monoxide, CO (Ag, Au, Zn, Pt, Pd, Ga, Ni).[13] CO has to be associated with dihydrogen to form syngas and go through the Fischer-Tropsch process before obtaining hydrocarbons, reused as fuels.[14] Copper is one of the few elements able to directly produce complex hydrocarbons through the electrochemical process. However, copper as a catalyst produces a large variety of hydrocarbons with low efficiency and low selectivity for each.[15]
A recent study performed by Song et al.[16] showed that a catalyst based on copper nanoparticles and dispersed on a graphitic material could produce ethanol with faradaic efficiency of 61% and a selectivity of 62% toward the carbon-based products (value extrapolated from the article’s data). Song et al. indicate that the synergistic effect between the carbon-based material and the copper nanoparticles is apparently responsible for the high electrocatalytic performance of the catalyst. Despite the high efficiency of their catalyst, the reported current density is relatively low, around 2 mA·cm-2 at -1.2 V vs RHE, making the catalyst not suitable for a commercial application. Commercial catalysts for CO2 reduction are expected to have current densities higher that 100 mA·cm-2 for faradaic efficiencies reaching at least 50%.[17]
The present study is using graphene nanoflakes (GNFs), a material developed in the Plasma Processing Laboratory, McGill University, back in 2011.[18] GNFs have proven to be an interesting carbon support for catalytic applications largely because of their outstanding crystallinity properties.[19] Different methods of functionalization and nanoparticles decoration have been developed and applied to the GNFs[20]–[22] while literature describes popular methods such as electrodeposition or solvothermal methods.[23], [24] The wet chemistry method initially developed by Yeager et al.[25] is chosen in this study to disperse copper-based nanoparticles having traces of oxygen and sulfur with diameter below 50 nm on the surface of the GNFs (Cu-GNFs) and thus synthesize an active catalyst toward the CO2 electroreduction.
Copper-based catalysts containing varying amounts of sulfur are known from literature to be selective toward the formation of formic acid.[26]–[29] However, these catalysts are either made by doping a bare copper surface or depositing copper sulfide particles on a copper surface, resulting in an exclusively metallic
catalyst. The approach adopted in the present study is to disperse the copper-based nanoparticles on a graphene support and thus use only a fraction of the metal while obtaining similar performance.
Catalysts with various amounts of copper, copper oxide and copper sulfide phases are synthesized and characterized in this study. Physical characterization aims to understand the structure and composition of the samples, while electrochemical characterization provides an insight on the electrocatalytic performance of the Cu-GNFs.

sections.heading: 2. Experimental methods
sections.text:
2.1.Catalyst preparation
Graphene nanoparticles grown using a thermal plasma method, thereafter called graphene nanoflakes (GNFs), are used to support and disperse copper catalyst nanoparticles, these nanostructures being referred to as Cu-GNFs. GNFs are grown using a thermal plasma method following Pristavita’s procedure.[30] Methane is injected in an inductively coupled thermal plasma (ICP) torch where molecules are decomposed into carbon and hydrogen atoms by the argon thermal plasma (typically 10,000 K in the main plasma zone). The ICP torch is connected to a water-cooled axisymmetric reactor with a conical expansion that allows a well-controlled flow line pattern and cooling of the plasma during expansion. This enables homogeneous nucleation of the atomic carbon precursor and growth of the specific GNF structures within a temperature window modeled to be between 4,900 K down to 3,700 K. The high temperature of the nucleation region and the extended residence time in the growth region enabled by the system geometry generate GNF structures with exceptional crystallinity downstream of the ICP torch (Figure 1).[31] The GNFs are deposited on the walls by thermophoretic forces and on the downstream collection plate of the reactor. A small flow of nitrogen (0.1 slpm) is typically added during the growth procedure along with methane, leading to a nitrogen functionalization content up to 2 at% on the surface of the GNFs. The GNFs structure consists of typically 5 to 20 atomic layers (10 on average) of stacked graphene with lateral dimensions in the order of 100 nm.
Figure 1: High resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) image of the single crystal graphene nano-flake structures in the present application, showing the continuous atomic plane organization of the graphene structure maintained throughout the sheet-like structures, each line in a given flake representing one atomic plane of carbon. Bottom insert: enlargement of a section of a flake showing an inter-planar distance of 0.33 nm corresponding to the atomic inter-planar distance between the honeycomb-structured graphene planes of graphite (Top-right insert).
The addition of the copper nanoparticles to the GNFs is made by chemical precipitation. GNFs are dispersed in a 1:1 mixture of water and ethanol. Various amounts of copper sulfate salt (CuSO4 from Sigma Aldrich ©) are dissolved in a water-ethanol solvent. The amount of salt added to the mixture is adjusted to obtain a final catalyst having from 20 to 50 wt% copper. The mixture is stirred until complete dissolution of the copper sulfate salt, and then dried in an oven at 80°C for 24h. The dried solid is collected before undergoing a pyrolysis step. The pyrolysis step is performed in a tubular quartz furnace at 700°C for an hour under a flow of 542 sccm of argon. The mass of the catalysts is controlled before and after pyrolysis. It can be noted that the GNFs do not degrade or decompose at the temperature used during the pyrolysis because of their
high level of crystallinity. Thermogravimetry analysis (TGA) made in air on pure GNF samples indicate a degradation temperature of 775°C, a temperature much higher than any other graphene-based materials evaluated. It is also important to note that no mass loss is observed at lower temperatures, contrary to graphene oxide (GO) or reduced graphene oxide (RGO) materials. 2.2.Physical characterization
The catalysts are also analyzed in terms of their structure and composition. Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM, using a FEI Tecnai G2 F20 200 kV Cryo-STEM, McGill University) is used for observing the catalysts at atomic level resolution and more particularly the copper nanoparticles for size distribution determination. The overall copper content in the different catalysts is determined by Neutron Activation Analysis (NAA, SLOWPOKE Laboratory, Institute of Nuclear Engineering, École Polytechnique de Montréal). The SLOWPOKE nuclear reactor is equipped with an Ortec GEM30185-P germanium semiconductor gamma-ray detector, an Ortec DSPEC ProTM multichannel analyzer, a Sartorius precision balance and the EPAA analysis software.[32] The elemental composition of the samples is analyzed by X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) on a Scientific K-Alpha XPS from Thermo
Scientific. An aluminum x-ray source is used on 400 μm size area. X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) is used to determine the crystalline phase of the copper nanoparticles in the samples and performed on a Brucker D8 Discovery X-Ray Diffractometer with a VANTEC detector, and having a copper Kα source.
2.3.Electrochemical characterization
The electrochemical characterization of the Cu-GNFs catalysts is realized in a custom made three-electrode set-up with different configurations for gas and electrolyte sampling. The counter electrode is a platinum wire separated to the other two electrodes by a Nafion membrane in order to avoid the oxidation of the products generated at the cathode. The reference electrode is silver/silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) containing saturated solution. The working electrode is a 1 cm by 1 cm carbon cloth piece covered by 1 mg·cm-2 catalyst. Nitrogen and carbon dioxide gases are bubbled through a sintered quartz sparger in the electrolyte composed of a 0.1 M potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3) solution. The electrolyte is prepared by dissolving the KHCO3 salt (Sigma Aldrich ©) into deionized water. Potentials are converted from Ag/AgCl to the reverse hydrogen electrode (RHE) using Nernst equation (Equation 1):

The catalysts are dispersed into an ink prior deposition on the working electrode. The catalyst ink consists of catalyst powder (5 mg), ethanol (1 mL) and Nafion (4 μL, 5 wt% solution from Sigma Aldrich ©). The ink is sonicated before series of 4 depositions (50 μL each), for a total volume of 200 μL deposited on the electrodes. The electrodes are dried for 24h in an oven at 80°C.
Linear Sweep Voltammetry (LSV) and Chrono-Amperometry (CA) are used to characterize the catalysts. LSV consists in recording the current density for a range of potential, while CA consist in holding a potential for a certain duration and measuring the current density. For both electrochemical analyses, the catalysts go
through a conditioning step under nitrogen bubbling in order to remove impurities on the catalyst surface. The conditioning step consists of repeated sweeps from 0.0 to -1.4 V vs RHE at a scan rate of 100 mV·s-1 until there is no variation from a voltammogram to the next one. LSVs are then recorded in electrolytes saturated with nitrogen and then carbon dioxide from 0.0 to -1.4 V vs RHE at a scan rate of 20 mV.s-1. Carbon dioxide is bubbled for 30 min in order to reach the saturation concentration in the electrolyte.
CA is performed by holding potentials of -0.6 and -0.9 V vs RHE for 2 hours whereas the current density is recorded. Gas and liquid products are generated during the CA and are quantified by Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) and Gas Chromatography (GC). NMR is performed on a Bruker Advance III HD 600 MHz instrument. NMR samples were prepared by mixing liquid analyte (500 μL), 12 mM DMSO solution in a 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (50 μL) and D2O (100 μL). A preliminary calibration is performed on the following five products: formate, methanol, acetate, ethanol and n-propanol. GC is performed on a Micro GC 490 (Agilent Technologies). A calibration is done on hydrogen, methane, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, ethylene and ethene standard gases.
The quantification of the gaseous and liquid products generated during the CO2 electroreduction is used to calculate the Faradaic Efficiency (FE) shown in Equation 2.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
3.1.Structure and composition of the Cu-GNFs
The Cu-GNFs are analysed by TEM where both GNFs and copper nanoparticles are observed, the copper appearing as the darkest particles on Figure 2. The flake shape of the stacked graphene is typical for the
GNF nanoparticles. Copper nanoparticles show a relatively wide size distribution, from a few tens of nanometers to several hundreds of nanometers for the largest particles. These are not homogenously dispersed on the GNFs, with areas containing more copper than others, that can be explained by the hydrophobic nature of the GNFs. Indeed, the GNFs see a partial agglomeration during the evaporation of the solvent, causing some areas to not be covered by the precipitating copper salt.
The high-resolution image shows a stacked crystalline GNF structure having roughly 15 atomic layers extending towards the top right of the figure, and a large zone of crystallinity within the Cu nanoparticle. This zone shows an inter-atomic spacing going from 0.24 to 0.28 nm which corresponds to either the (111) atomic plane of tetragonal CuO, the (111) atomic plane of cubic Cu2O or the (200) atomic plane of cubic Cu2S. The composition of areas containing copper and areas containing only the GNFs is analyzed by Energy Dispersive Spectrometry (EDS) and shown on Figure 3. The analysis reveals the presence of Carbon, Oxygen, Copper and Sulfur. Areas containing only GNFs are mostly composed of carbon, with traces of copper due to the TEM support grid made in copper and covered by a thin layer of carbon. The copper nanoparticles are thus composed of copper and sulfur, suggesting the presence of copper sulfide.
Figure 3: EDS spectrum on area containing copper nanoparticles (top, green line) and area containing only GNFs (bottom, black line)
The elemental composition of the surface of the Cu-GNFs reveal the presence of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and copper as seen on the XPS survey on Figure 4 for the sample Cu-GNF2. High-resolution peaks of the different elements are recorded and analyzed to determine the chemical state of the elements through deconvolution as shown on Figure 5 also for the sample Cu-GNF2. Carbon is mostly in sp2 hybridized state (Figure 5a), corresponding to the graphitic form of carbon, with small amounts of carbon bonded to nitrogen and oxygen. Carbon forms the majority of the elemental composition of the surface of the particles. This is expected from the graphene support holding the Cu nanoparticles. One can note for example that high resolution scans of Figure 2b effectively indicate zones of the particle covered with graphene layers, while Figure 2a shows particles with attached graphene-like structures at their surface. Nitrogen is found is small amounts under the four different forms typically found in graphitic structures: pyridinic, pyrrolic,
quaternary and oxidized nitrogen (Figure 5b). Nitrogen is coming from the small flow of nitrogen added for functionalization during the GNF growth in the thermal plasma reactor. It was shown by Wu et al. that nitrogen in the pyridinic form promotes the CO2 reduction.[33] Pyridinic nitrogen accounts between 14.3%- 44.4% of the nitrogen functionalization, as indicated in Table 3 showing the relative amounts of various species. Oxygen (Figure 5c) is present in the samples for several reasons: contamination in the thermal plasma reactor during the GNFs growth, contact of the powder with air, the wet chemistry method and the oxidation of the copper nanoparticles. It can also be noted that Cu-GNF1 contains some adsorbed humidity on its surface, from Table 3: Relative amounts of Carbon, Nitrogen, Oxygen and Copper states from deconvolution of the high-resolution peaks.Table 3, where the relative amounts of the detected elements are detailed for each sample.
Figure 4: XPS Survey for Cu-GNF2.
Sulfur was detected by EDS during the TEM analysis, as seen on Figure 3, but only a very weak signal is detected by XPS at the typical binding energy of 162 eV for sulfur S 2p. XPS is a technique characterizing
only a very thin surface layer of the sample surface. The absence of a meaningful signature of sulfur in the XPS analysis could be related to its presence essentially in the core of the nanoparticles or a nonhomogeneous distribution of the copper sulfide phase in the sample. The copper nanoparticles are synthesized from CuSO4. The temperature of 700°C used in the pyrolysis step is expected to evaporate the SO2 groups and then reduce copper oxide to copper in presence of the carbon material, however some sulfur may be trapped inside the core of the nanoparticles to form copper sulfide. Some nanoparticles could also be preferentially made of metallic copper while other mostly of copper sulfide.
The actual copper content in the bulk of the samples is determined by NAA. The amount of copper in the catalysts is 17.6, 26.6, 41.4 and 52.6 wt% for Cu-GNF1,2,3 and 4 respectively. These values show that the synthesis process delivers the expected amount of copper with an error between -12% and +5%.
Figure 5: High-resolution XPS peaks of (a) Carbon C1s, (b) Nitrogen N1s, (c) Oxygen O1s and (d) Copper Cu2p for sample Cu-GNF2.

The XPS data of Figure 5 are used to evaluate the elemental composition at the surface of the Cu-GNF catalysts. Copper in the catalyst samples have two chemical states which are located at 954.0 and 952.0 eV (Figure 5d). The peak located at 954.0 eV corresponds without any doubt to copper oxide CuO due to its peak location and satellite shape.[34] The identification of the chemical state from the peak at 952.0 eV can be more difficult, because metallic copper, copper oxide Cu2O and copper sulfide Cu2S present very similar signals in XPS. However, the non-homogeneous distribution of sulfur, the analysis of the elemental composition (Table 2) and the relative amounts (Table 3) from copper and oxygen tend to support the presence of metallic copper in the samples. It can be noted from Table 3 that the samples Cu-GNF2 and Cu-GNF3 contain nearly half of the overall surface-based copper in metallic form while Cu-GNF1 and CuGNF4 have mostly oxidized copper. XPS being a surface analysis, it is possible that the copper nanoparticles in Cu-GNF2 and Cu-GNF3 have a thinner oxide layer compared to the ones in Cu-GNF1 and Cu-GNF4.

The Cu-GNFs are analyzed by XRD to investigate the crystalline structure of the copper nanoparticles as seen on Figure 6. Indeed, the previous techniques used (TEM, EDS and XPS) show the possibility to have metallic copper, copper oxide and/or copper sulfide in the samples. The typical peaks for the GNFs are observed on the diffractograms, with a broad peak at 25° and peaks located at 42°, 72° and 88°[18] which are overlapping with peaks associated to metallic copper. The most intense peaks observed on the diffractogram are from metallic copper, located at 43°, 50°, 74°, and 90°.[35] The least intense peaks include phases of copper oxide and sulfide, whose relative amounts are depicted in Table 4. It can be noted that the typical interplanar distances of copper oxide and copper sulfide have been observed between 0.24 nm and 0.28 nm using TEM, these values being larger than the typical interplanar of metallic copper which is 0.21 nm.

It can be noted that the samples Cu-GNF2 and Cu-GNF3 contain copper sulfide while Cu-GNF1 and CuGNF4 contain copper oxide. Metallic copper is present in all the samples, with increasing percentage. Comparing with XPS results, the samples containing solely copper sulfide also contained the lowest amount
of oxygen, and the lowest amount of copper bonded to oxygen. The presence of copper oxide by XPS on samples Cu-GNF2 and Cu-GNF3 which was not detected by XRD can be explained by a thin and amorphous oxide layer on these samples. The XRD spectra also show an increasing amount of metallic copper in the samples synthesized with increasing amount of copper sulfate. This analysis suggests that changing the amount of copper sulfate while keeping the other synthesis parameters constant has a great impact on the composition of the samples, and possibly on the performance of the catalysts.
3.2.Electrochemical characterization of the catalysts
The Cu-GNF samples are tested for the electroreduction of CO2 by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), first under nitrogen and then under CO2 bubbling. Three runs are recorded and compiled for each condition, an example being seen on Figure 7 for Cu-GNF2. The onset potential and current density for each catalyst is reported in Table 5. The onset potential is typically defined as the potential where the corrected current density is no longer null. In the present case, the onset potential is defined as the potential where the current density is reaching a value more negative with CO2 bubbling compared to nitrogen bubbling. The current density reported in Table 5 is measured at -0.6 and -0.9 V vs RHE, potentials at which chronoamperometry (CA) is performed.
The catalysts all have a higher current density under the CO2 bubbling compared to nitrogen bubbling, suggesting an activity toward the CO2 reduction. The analysis of the LSVs provides a screening technique to compare the electrochemical performance of the different catalysts, and selection of the best one. CuGNF2 has the highest onset potential among the catalysts, while exhibiting high values of current density at both -0.6 and -0.9 V vs RHE.

Each catalyst undergoes CA for the two potentials of -0.6 and -0.9 V vs RHE during two hours. The liquid products are identified and quantified by NMR. Among the different products tested, formate and npropanol were the major products detected, with a few traces of other products, such as carbon monoxide and ethanol, close to the detection limits. Due to the low amount of these other products, and a contribution of less than 0.1% to the faradaic efficiency, they are not taken into account in the results nor represented on Figure 8 for the different catalysts.
One could have expected to observe a higher amount of ethanol compared to n-propanol in these conditions. The contamination of the samples with n-propanol can already be excluded to explain this phenomenon because the use of common organics such as ethanol, isopropanol or acetone is prohibited to rinse the electrochemical cell and the analysis tubes. Geioushy et al. proposed an electrocatalyst made of graphene, zinc oxide and copper oxide exhibiting a high selectivity toward propanol.[36] With a faradaic efficiency of 30% toward n-propanol at a potential of -0.9 V vs Ag/AgCl, they did not defined the mechanisms pathway explaining the higher production of n-propanol, but believed the strong interaction between zinc oxide, copper oxide with graphene was responsible of this observation. Similar structure with copper oxide and graphene are found in the Cu-GNF catalysts and may be responsible for the higher amount of n-propanol compared to ethanol.
In all of the conditions, formate is generated with more than 99% selectivity among liquid products, while Cu-GNF2 exhibits the best performance in terms of faradaic efficiency. The efficiency is reaching up to 40% toward formate at the potential of -0.6 V vs RHE.
Figure 8: Faradaic efficiency toward formate (green, top) and n-propanol (black, bottom) at -0.6 and -0.9 V vs RHE for the Cu-GNFs.
It appears that increasing the overall amount of copper in the catalysts is not directly correlated to an improvement in the electrocatalytic activity toward the CO2 reduction. Similarly, increasing amount of metallic copper does not correlate with the catalysts performance. Cu-GNF2 is the catalyst containing the highest amount of copper sulfide. Literature suggests that copper nanoparticles doped with sulfur are more selective toward formate generation.[37], [38] However, copper sulfide does not explain by itself the difference of performance between the samples, and copper oxide has also to be taken into account. [39]
Cu-GNF2 is studied in more details due to its better performance compared to the other samples. CA is performed at -0.6, -0.7, -0.8 and -0.9 V vs RHE in order to find the potential where both faradaic efficiency and current density are maximized, as shown on Figure 9. The highest efficiency toward formate generation is observed at -0.6 V vs RHE, representing a low overpotential of 0.375 V compared to the redox potential of the couple CO2/HCOO- (-0.225 V). Hydrogen, CO2 and air are detected as gases, but H2 is the only gas produced through electrochemistry and counted for in the calculation of the Faradaic Efficiency. Hydrogen
formation is a competitive process to the CO2 reduction and has to be minimized to favor formate generation. The overall Faradaic efficiency varies between 91% at -0.9V vs RHE and 96% at -0.6 V vs RHE. The FE is lower than 100% because of traces of products that are not counted in the calculation, losses in the set-up, and measurement error.
Figure 9: Faradaic efficiency towards hydrogen (blue, top), formate (green, middle), and n-propanol (black, bottom) at -0.6, -0.7, -0.8 and -0.9 V vs RHE for Cu-GNF2.
The performance of the catalysts described in this study are to be put in perspective with similar studies.[26]– [29], [37], [38]. Both of these studies examined sulfide copper as an electrocatalyst towards the CO2 reduction. Zhu et al. studied Cu2S electrodeposited on copper foam, while Phillips et al. and Deng et al. deposited copper sulfide particles on copper foil. These catalysts presents the main drawback of being composed of almost pure copper, which is mostly non-accessible for catalyst application compared to the use of nanoparticles. For Zhu et al., the catalyst also requires a higher potential of -1.4 V vs RHE compared to - 0.6 V vs RHE in the present study showing a reduction of CO2 with same faradaic efficiency. Shinagawa et al. suggested a catalyst closer in its structure to the Cu-GNFs used here, their catalyst consisting of Cu2S
nanoparticles dispersed on Vulcan carbon black with a comparison made to pure Cu2S nanoparticles. Their catalyst contained lower metallic content than the Cu-GNFs, with 5 wt% of Cu2S, and obtained similar faradaic efficiency at same potential. However, a higher catalyst loading (1.5 vs 1.0 mg.cm-2) was used and a lower current density of -2.5 mA.cm-2 was obtained. While Shinagawa et al. tailored their catalysts to contain pure Cu2S nanoparticles, the Cu-GNFs have metallic, oxide and sulfide forms of copper. Also, part of copper sulfide in the Cu-GNFs may be trapped inside metallic copper nanoparticles, suggested by the absence of a meaningful sulfur signal by XPS. This suggests that Cu-GNFs performance could be improved by decreasing the amount of overall copper in the catalysts and tailoring the process to obtain preferentially Cu2S nanoparticles dispersed on the GNFs. Shinagawa et al. obtained slightly higher faradaic efficiency for their pure Cu2S catalysts, with a higher current density than their previous catalysts. The performance from the copper-based catalysts from literature is summarized in Table 6 and compared with Cu-GNF2.
From their observation and the present study, it shows that it is feasible to obtain similar performance by using 7 to 20 times less copper sulfide in the catalyst by dispersing it on a carbon support under the form of nanoparticles, and reduce the overall amount of copper up to 70%.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
Catalysts made of metallic copper and copper sulfide nanoparticles deposited on graphene nanoflakes are produced with an easy and scalable wet-chemistry method followed by pyrolysis step. One of the catalysts produced (Cu-GNF2) offers interesting electrochemical properties with low overpotential, high current densities and faradaic efficiencies going up to 40% towards formate production. This specific catalyst is characterized by a high amount of copper sulfide in its composition. The results from the study as well as comparison with literature suggests that promoting Cu2S nanoparticles over metallic copper could improve the performance of the Cu-GNF catalysts by decreasing the overall amount of metal. The simple method of catalyst production can be extended to other non-noble metal such as tin or lead which exhibit promising performance in the CO2 electroreduction.
Industrial CO2 electrolyzer require catalysts with higher faradaic efficiency and higher current densities which can be achieved through several strategies. Higher faradaic efficiency could be attained by using pure Cu2S nanoparticles instead of a combination of metallic and sulfide copper, or switching to another metal like tin or lead. Higher current densities are naturally reached when the catalyst is transferred from a three-electrode set-up to an actual electrolyzer. Indeed, the catalyst vicinity in the three-electrode set-up gets rapidly depleted in CO2 even with magnetic agitation while there are higher flows of CO2 on the surface of the catalyst in an electrolyzer. Adequate current densities will also depend on parameters such as catalyst loading, pressure of the gas, temperature of the electrolyte in the electrolyzer, or the addition of ionic liquids to the catalyst.
